h: A horn from a king and a ghostly Green Lady
p: The Burnett family's link with the land goes back to the 14th century, when Robert the Bruce granted lands to Alexander Burnard as a reward for loyal service. The ivory Horn of Leys, said to have been given by the king as a symbol of that gift, is kept in the castle, and it is a remarkable thing to see.

Every Scottish castle needs a ghost, and Crathes has the Green Lady, said to haunt one of the rooms. Whether you believe it or not, the stories make a great talking point for kids as they climb the twisty stairs.

The gardens are a big draw. The walled garden is divided into themed sections, and the giant clipped yew hedges, planted in the early 1700s, are some of the oldest features in the grounds. Gardeners can spend hours here, especially in summer when the borders are at their best.
Allow at least half a day to see the castle, garden and a woodland trail. Bring something warm, as Deeside can be breezy even in summer.

Near Crathes, the Royal Deeside Railway runs short heritage trips, so check before you go. Banchory is a pleasant small town with cafés and shops, and just south of it, at the Bridge of Feugh, you can watch salmon leaping up the falls at the right time of year. Drum Castle, another National Trust for Scotland property, is also close by, while heading further up the Dee takes you to Ballater and towards Balmoral and the Cairngorms.
